subject: english-language
title: Two Words and Telegrams
welcome_lead: Grammar arrives. Watch two-word combinations bloom and telegraphic speech compress meaning to its core.
meta_desc: Two-word stage, telegraphic speech and pivot grammars in child language acquisition at A-Level.
final_note: You have witnessed grammar emerging — pivots, semantic relations and the first telegrams of thought.

concepts.def: 18-24 months: combinations like 'more milk', 'daddy go' showing emergent syntax.
24-30 months: 3-4 word utterances missing function words (daddy go work), like an old telegram.
Martin Braine's analysis (1963) of two-word speech using high-frequency pivot words plus open class items.
Roger Brown's (1973) categories: agent-action, action-object, possessor-possession etc.
Mean Length of Utterance — average number of morphemes per utterance, an index of grammatical development.
Telegraphic speech drops articles, auxiliaries and inflections, keeping content words.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Around 18 months children combine two words. Braine observed many followed a pivot + open pattern: a small set of high-frequency words (more, allgone) combined with content words.

Brown's semantic relations capture the meanings expressed: agent-action (baby fall), possession (mummy shoe).

By 24-30 months utterances grow to 3-4 words but function morphemes are still scarce: daddy go work, doggy eat bone.

Brown (1973) traced the order in which grammatical morphemes are mastered — present progressive -ing first, then plural -s, then irregular past.
Brown's MLU counts morphemes per utterance averaged over a sample. He proposed five stages, with MLU moving from 1.0 (one-word) toward 4.0+ as complex syntax emerges.
